text.p: This is how major world bond markets were trading in late European business on Monday.

GERMANY - German Bunds remained moderately weak in late trade on Monday in what traders called a welcome consolidation of recent gains. The December Bund future on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) was trading at 98.69, down 0.05 from Friday's settlement price.

BRITAIN - Gilts ended a dull session marginally ahead having spent most of the day meandering in a tight trading range. The December long gilt future on LIFFE was trading at 108-21/32, up 03/32 from Friday's settlement price.

FRANCE - French December bond futures traded in a narrow range on Monday, taking a breather after last week's rally, to settle little changed despite a U.S. bond slide late in the session. The December notional bond future on the MATIF in Paris settled at 124.82 down 0.02 from Friday's settlement price.

ITALY - Italian bonds and futures ended quietly lower but had pared some losses by the close after surging last week on euphoria for Italy's maxi-budget for Europe. The December bond future on LIFFE was trading at 121.60 down 0.30 from Friday's settlement price.

UNITED STATES - U.S. Treasury prices erased an early advance and turned lower after the government reported a surprising jump in August single-family home sales. The December Treasury bond future on the Chicago Board of Trade was trading at 109-06/32, down 08/32 from Friday's settlement price. The long bond was quoted to yield 6.93 percent.

JAPAN - Key December Japanese government bond (JGB) futures staged a sharp rise to regain the 122 level on Monday after rate comments by Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita, which reached the market early in the morning. In after hours trading the December future on LIFFE was trading at 122.15, up 0.53 from Friday's settlement price on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

EUROBONDS - The City of Yokohama launched its long-awaited $200 million 10-year Eurobond on Monday at a spread of 27 basis points over U.S. Treasury notes. An official at lead manager Tokyo-Mitsubishi said the deal had gone well and was heavily oversubscribed. He said around 60 percent of the paper went to European and British accounts, with 25 to 30 percent placed with non-Japan Asian investors.
Other syndicate managers said the Yokohama issue was well-received, with investors attracted by its Japanese government-guarantee which gave it a triple-A rating.
